title: He didn’t just betray Jesus.
paragraphs:
He didn’t just betray Jesus.
He misread Him.
Thirty pieces of silver… or a shattered expectation?

Judas walked with Christ. Heard the sermons. Saw the miracles.
This wasn’t a random sinner in the crowd.
This was someone close.
And that’s what makes it heavier.

Some say it was greed.
Judas Iscariot held the money bag (John 12:6). He knew the weight of coins… and the pull of them.
But here’s what we miss…

What if it wasn’t just greed?
What if it was disillusionment?

Judas expected a conquering King.
A political Messiah.
A throne, not a cross.
But Jesus Christ kept talking about surrender… suffering… dying.
That doesn’t sell well to a man who wants power.

So maybe Judas didn’t just sell Jesus—
he tried to force Him.

Push Him into a corner.
Trigger the revolution.
Make Him prove He was the Messiah on Judas’ terms.
But heaven doesn’t move on human manipulation.

And when Jesus didn’t fight back…
when He chose the cross instead of the sword…
Judas realized too late—

He didn’t betray a weak Savior.
He betrayed a holy one.

Matthew 27 says he felt remorse.
He returned the silver.
But remorse is not the same as repentance.

One leads to despair.
The other leads to a Savior.
And that’s where the story splits.
Peter the Apostle also failed Jesus. Publicly. Painfully.

But Peter ran toward grace.
Judas ran away from it.

Same failure category.
Different response.
And that changes everything.
So was it greed or disillusionment?

Yes.
And deeper still—
a heart that wanted Jesus… but on its own terms.
Let this hit you:

You can follow Jesus closely…
and still resist the kind of King He truly is.
But here’s the Gospel—

Jesus didn’t go to the cross because Judas betrayed Him.
He went because we needed saving.
Even betrayal was woven into redemption.
Even sin became the stage for grace.

If you’ve been disappointed with God…
if He didn’t meet your expectations…
Don’t walk away like Judas.
Run back.

The cross still stands.
The tomb is still empty.
And mercy is still open.
